content.comment_body: Hello, how many [product_name] devices can be set up in a daisy chain using an Ethernet switch for each device, since they are installed far apart from one another? Thank you.

A single [product_name] can be connected to up to 16 other [product_name] devices. Of these, 8 connections are static and the rest are dynamic. Note that a standard Ethernet switch is not a repeater, so the maximum cable length between each [product_name] is 100 meters.
Thank you for your reply. I have attached my proposed plan for the new project. Could you please provide feedback on whether this layout is feasible? Thanks.

Communication without a repeater is possible between certain [product_name] units, such as 1, 2, and 3, or 2 and 3, or 3 and 4. The 100-meter limit is based on a theoretical value provided by [company_name]. In practice, you may be able to exceed 100 meters, but that can only be confirmed by testing.
If the setup doesn't work because the distance is too great, are there alternative solutions available? My experience with networking is limited.
In that case, you should install repeaters between switches.

For simple applications, you can group up to 8 [product_name] devices in each group. I've configured 15 devices across 4 groups, each installed at different locations, all on the same network using switches and optical converters. This worked well in an airport environment.
When you mention a repeater, are you referring to an RJ45 optical media converter?
[user_name], could you share more details about your system? Thanks.

That configuration works. But why use so many switches? If only [product_name] devices are connected to SW1-SW5, you could link [product_name] devices 1 and 2 directly to SW3, removing SW1 and SW2. No need for repeaters. If it's necessary to connect SW5 to SW4, two 5-port Fast Ethernet (100 Mbit) switches will suffice. For example: [product_name]1 — SW3 port1; [product_name]2 — SW3 port2; [product_name]3 — SW3 port3; SW4 — SW3 port4; [product_name]4 — SW4 port1; SW5 — SW4 port5. If SW5 can connect to SW3 with a cable under 100 m, SW4 isn't necessary. Cat5e cable is enough; no need for gigabit-capable CAT6.

Regarding switches, the information is not entirely accurate. For a long time, I used a standard 4-port switch at home to boost my internet signal. When my internet was weak and I couldn't access my desktop network board, adding the switch improved connectivity enough to use the network. While it wasn't as strong as a repeater, it did not significantly reduce signal strength. I haven't tried connecting [product_name] devices at distances greater than 10-20 meters, but I see no technical barriers for using a switch in such setups.
Hello [user_name], remember that using a repeater, hub, or switch will lower the available network bandwidth.

analysis.insight_summary: Participants are discussing how many [product_name] devices can be networked together in a daisy chain over long distances, focusing on both the theoretical and practical limitations of Ethernet. They highlight challenges with network design, including device connection limits and cable length, and debate the role of switches versus repeaters and media converters. There is uncertainty around networking components and a desire for practical solutions that are viable for large physical deployments.
analysis.user_expectations: The primary expectation is clear guidance on how many [product_name] devices can be networked together, useful advice for configuring systems where devices are far apart, and accessible solutions for issues that arise with standard networking approaches. Users are looking for scalable, reliable methods without requiring advanced networking expertise.
